name: Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery
overview: National museum on Independence Drive, Waigani, Port Moresby, holding tens of thousands of artefacts from PNG's 22 provinces (Business Advantage PNG, Robert Upe, 18 May 2020). Wikipedia says it holds over 50,000 ethnographic objects.

Wikipedia traces its origins to a Board of Trustees formed in 1954 and the Public Museums and Art Galleries Ordinance of 1956. Collections sat in disused government buildings and an old hospital from 1960. Construction of a purpose-built museum began in 1975 with partial Australian government funding, and it opened to the public on 27 June 1977.
The original 1974 building was by Martin Fowler (Architectus, 14 November 2018).
funding_verdict: Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery: statutory body: Australian grants paid for the building and its upgrade

name: Museo del Barro
overview: Museum of popular, indigenous and contemporary art at Grabadores del Cabichuí 2716, between Cañada and Emeterio Miranda, in the Isla de Francia neighbourhood of Asunción. It is part of the Centro de Artes Visuales (CAV), which also holds the Museo de Arte Indígena and the Museo Paraguayo de Arte Contemporáneo (MPAC).

The museum was created in 1979, the year construction of its first building began, and opened in San Lorenzo in 1980 with about 800 pieces of popular ceramics from Ita and Tobatí and Guaraní archaeological ceramics. Ysanne Gayet, Carlos Colombino and Osvaldo Salerno started the San Lorenzo opening, and it moved to Asunción in 1983 and settled permanently in the CAV in 1988 (museum history page).

Olga Blinder and Carlos Colombino created the Colección Circulante in 1972, the origin of the MPAC collection. Ticio Escobar gathered and curated the collection behind the Museo de Arte Indígena (museum history page).
funding_verdict: Museo del Barro: private foundation museum, with bank sponsors, an embassy and named individual friends

name: MAC Lima
overview: Museum of modern and contemporary art at Av. Grau 1511 in Barranco, Lima, with three galleries of 100, 200 and 1,000 square metres in an industrial-style building surrounded by a terrace and a park (MAC Lima).
It opened in late January 2013 on the site of the former Barranco Zoo and its artificial lake, which closed in 1970 (English Wikipedia); Spanish Wikipedia gives 23 January 2013.

It is run by the Instituto de Arte Contemporáneo (IAC), founded in Lima on 11 June 1955, which decided in the late 1980s to build a museum for its collection (Spanish Wikipedia). The IAC opened in the former Galería de Lima premises, moved to Casa Mujica in 1966 and used the Museum of Italian Art building from 1969 to 1972 (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: MAC Lima: private non-profit on municipal land: self-generated income, a friends' programme, a telecom foundation and a one-off Getty grant
wider_context: In February 2018 the museum showed "Canon: Vírgenes de la Puerta" by Juan José Barboza-Gubo and Andrew Mroczek, to 1 April. A CitizenGo petition addressed to the museum's then director Enrique Stiglich, to the head of the Spanish aid agency and to Spain's ambassador demanded the closing of this show and a parallel one at the Cultural Center of Spain; it had more than 20,000 signatures by 27 February. The Advocate names Tradición y Acción por un Perú Mayor, Revuelta Contra el Arte Moderno and the Asociación Antonin Scalia as the groups behind the attack (The Advocate).
Conservative groups and congressman Carlos Tubino called the show blasphemous, which led to bill 2450 to criminalise religious defamation; the museum defended the works in public (Spanish Wikipedia).

name: Museo Larco
overview: Privately owned museum of pre-Columbian art in a former mansion in Pueblo Libre, Lima, at Av. Simón Bolívar 1515 (Wikipedia, Hispania Nostra directory).

Rafael Larco Hoyle founded it on 28 July 1926 as the Museo Chiclín near Trujillo, building on the collection of his father, Rafael Larco Herrera. It moved to Lima in the 1950s and became the Museo Arqueológico Rafael Larco Herrera (Spanish Wikipedia).
Its formal name, Museo Arqueológico Rafael Larco Herrera, honours the founder's father. After Larco Hoyle died in 1966 his daughter Isabel Larco took over the general management (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo Larco: private museum

name: Ateneo Art Gallery
overview: University art museum in the Soledad V. Pangilinan Arts Wing of Areté, Ateneo de Manila University, Katipunan Avenue, Loyola Heights, Quezon City.

Established in 1960 around the collection of Fernando Zóbel, a painter, art scholar and Ateneo teacher, who donated over 200 artworks as a study collection for students (Wikipedia). The Quezon City government listing calls it the first museum of Philippine modern art.
It first sat in Bellarmine Hall in 1961, moved to the ground floor of Rizal Library in 1967 and moved to the Arts Wing in Areté in 2017 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Ateneo Art Gallery: university museum: Ateneo de Manila University, with partners for its awards

name: Metropolitan Museum of Manila
overview: Non-profit museum of contemporary art, also called "The M", at the MK Tan Centre, 30th Street, Bonifacio Global City, Taguig (Metropolitan Museum of Manila).

Wikipedia dates its establishment to 3 October 1976 at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas complex in Malate, Manila. The Metropolitan Museum of Manila Foundation, Inc. was set up in 1979 by former First Lady Imelda Marcos and businessman Bienvenido Tantoco Sr., and in September 1986 the museum became a non-government organisation (Wikipedia).
The museum site says it opened its new home in Bonifacio Global City in October 2022. The Urban Roamer blog (20 July 2025) places it next to the JY Campos Centre, the headquarters of NutriAsia.
funding_verdict: Metropolitan Museum of Manila: non-government foundation, formerly subsidised by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas; chaired by NutriAsia founder Joselito Campos Jr.
wider_context: 2018 NutriAsia strike (Wikipedia): workers hired through the contractor B-Mirk, citing contractualisation and unsafe conditions, formed a union at NutriAsia's Marilao plant and its officers were laid off. On 23 February 2018 the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) ordered NutriAsia to give regular employment to 914 workers hired through three contractors as labour-only subcontracting; NutriAsia rejected that reading. On 25 June 2018 DOLE Region 3 reversed the finding.

On 30 June 2018 police dispersed about 300 people at the end of an ecumenical mass at the picket. At least 30 people were injured and 19 were arrested, 14 workers or supporters and five journalists. DOLE condemned the dispersal (Wikipedia).

The strike and dispersal took place at NutriAsia's plant, not at the museum. NutriAsia's founder Joselito Campos Jr. chairs the museum's board, and the Urban Roamer blog names NutriAsia as a founding benefactor.

press_items.outlet: Asia News Network, from the Philippine Daily Inquirer
press_items.title: Lala Singian, "Let's talk about the Banksy controversy in Manila" (23 May 2024)
Chad Rialp, "Banksy Universe Was Never Pre-Approved" (26 April 2024)
Joseph Gonzales, "Banksy bile" (28 April 2024), column "Looking Askance"

name: MOCAK
overview: Museum of Contemporary Art on Lipowa Street in Kraków, about 3 km from the city centre, on a demolished part of Oskar Schindler's former factory site (Wikipedia).

Established on 1 February 2010 and opened on 19 May 2011. Maria Anna (Masza) Potocka was its first director (Wikipedia). The museum's site describes it as an institution of culture of the City of Kraków.
Building designed by Claudio Nardi, with 4,000 square metres of exhibition space in a 10,000 square metre complex (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: MOCAK: public: an institution of culture of the City of Kraków, with Ministry of Culture grants and EU funds for the building

press_items.title: no named author, "Adam Budak dismissed as director of MOCAK amid controversy" (18 May 2026)

name: Belarusian Council for Culture (Rada Kultury)
overview: Exile network of Belarusian cultural experts, managers and artists, described by itself as "a community of experts, managers, and artists" that works to rebuild Belarusian cultural life under repression and emigration.
Registered in Estonia since October 2020 as MTÜ Valgevene Kultuuri Assotsiatsioon (registry code 80587137), with its legal address at Aru tn 21-8, Tallinn (stated by the council).
Granted human rights organisation status in May 2023 (stated by the council).
funding_verdict: Belarusian Council for Culture: mainly EU-funded: European Union grants through ArtPower Belarus, with the Danish Cultural Institute as partner
wider_context: Belarus declared the council an "extremist formation": the council's site says the Ministry of Internal Affairs did so, and a Minsk court ruled its materials "extremist". Reform.news reported on 24 April 2026 that the State Security Committee (KGB) added the council, the projects Mahistrat, Vasminoh and ArtPower Belarus, and the Foundation of the Belarusian Council for Culture to its list on 9 April 2026, and listed eleven individuals as associated with them, including Siarhiej Budkin and Elina Kałnibałockaja.
Reform.news reported human rights defenders saying investigators are looking for "foreign funding", with searches, detentions and interrogations of people linked to cultural organisations.
The council is registered in Estonia and names the European Union as the funder of ArtPower Belarus; the designation comes from Belarusian authorities (stated by the council; Reform.news).

name: Kupalaŭcy (Free Kupala Theatre in exile)
overview: Belarusian-language theatre troupe in exile. The question of a stationary venue was never resolved, and its seventh season (2026) has premieres in Kraków, Wrocław and Warsaw (Reform.news, 31 January 2026; Reform.news, 30 July 2026).

Formed in 2020 after dismissals at the Yanka Kupala National Academic Theatre in Minsk in August. Wikipedia gives 26 August 2020 as the founding date, and the troupe debuted on 6 October 2020 with "Tutejshyya" at the OK16 venue, without sets or costumes (Reform.news, 31 January 2026).
Wikipedia says director-general Pavel Latushko was fired on 17 August 2020 and 58 actors and staff were dismissed on 26 August 2020.
funding_verdict: Kupalaŭcy: ticket sales, diaspora tax donations and project support

name: Museum of Free Belarus
overview: Museum of the 2020 Belarusian protest movement at ul. Foksal 11 in central Warsaw (Radio Svaboda).
A project of the National Anti-Crisis Management, led by Pavel Latushka, with support from Polish authorities. It began operating on 17 July 2022 (Radio Svaboda, 17 July 2022).
Premises: the Warsaw municipality provided over 367 square metres (National Anti-Crisis Management page, 14 May 2023).
funding_verdict: Museum of Free Belarus: exile political project: Polish public premises and grant, plus private donations

name: BWA Wrocław
overview: Public contemporary art institution (BWA Wrocław, Galerie Sztuki Współczesnej) with galleries across Wrocław: BWA Wrocław Główny, Dizajn, Studio and SIC!, plus the art magazine "Biuro" (City of Wrocław, 2020).

Its gallery Awangarda was built in the early 1970s on the site of the Hatzfeldt Palace at ul. Wita Stwosza, an 18th-century palace whose final design is credited to Carl Gotthard Langhans and which was badly damaged in 1945 (City of Wrocław, 8 September 2020).

In October 2018 the gallery left that building, which experts found in poor condition with some areas at risk of collapse, for about 1,000 to 1,200 square metres in the Wrocław Główny railway station (City of Wrocław, October 2018).
funding_verdict: BWA Wrocław: public: basic subsidy including the City of Wrocław's

name: Museo de Arte de Ponce
overview: Art museum at 2325 Avenida Las Américas (renamed Luis A. Ferré Boulevard), Ponce, Puerto Rico, owned by Fundación Luis A. Ferré, Inc. (Wikipedia).

Founded by industrialist Luis A. Ferré. It opened on 3 January 1959 in a house at 70 Cristina Street with 72 works, and moved to its current building on Avenida Las Américas, which opened on 28 December 1965 (Wikipedia).

The building was designed by Edward Durell Stone, with hexagonal galleries that let daylight in through their corners (Wikipedia). A 2010 annex added an education space, library, archives, conservation laboratory, storage area, shop and restaurant (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte de Ponce: private foundation museum, funded by founding families, individual patrons and corporate donors

name: Les Ateliers Sahm
overview: Contemporary art centre with its headquarters in Mpissa-Bacongo, in the second arrondissement of Brazzaville (ADIAC, 2023).
Founded by the artist and writer Bill Kouélany (Wikipedia). It opened in September 2012 (Almayuda) under his artistic direction (Contemporary And).
Facilities: an exhibition and screening room, a space for art criticism, a media archive, four workshop rooms and an esplanade for events (Almayuda).
funding_verdict: Les Ateliers Sahm: project-funded: a foundation, the Institut Français and the European Union fund individual programmes

name: Ploshchad Mira Museum Centre
overview: Museum and contemporary art centre at Ploshchad Mira 1, on the Yenisei embankment in Krasnoyarsk (Putevka).

Opened on 17 April 1987 as the 13th branch of the Central V.I. Lenin Museum, the only one in Siberia and the Russian Far East. It became the Krasnoyarsk Cultural-Historical Museum Centre in 1991 and was renamed Ploshchad Mira (Peace Square) in 2017 (Russian Wikipedia).
The Krasnoyarsk Museum Biennale has run since 1995, and Museum Night has been held twice a year since 2002, the first in Russia (Snob; Russian Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Ploshchad Mira Museum Centre: mainly public: the Krasnoyarsk Krai regional government, with earned income, grants and local business

name: AZ Museum (Anatoly Zverev Museum)
overview: Private single-artist museum at 2nd Tverskaya-Yamskaya 20-22, Moscow, between the Mayakovskaya and Belorusskaya metro stations (museum site). Snob describes silver letters on a beige marble facade near Mayakovsky Square.

Opened in May 2015. Natalia Opaleva is founder and general director, and Polina Lobachevskaya is co-organiser and art director (Vedomosti, Snob, Interfax). Snob says Lobachevskaya had curated a major Zverev show at the Tretyakov Gallery in 1999.
Named for the artist Anatoly Zverev. Snob describes the facade lettering "AZ" as his initials.
funding_verdict: AZ Museum: self-funded: the founder's own money
wider_context: Lanta-Bank, where Forbes Russia described Opaleva as vice-president in 2016: OpenSanctions says the bank "is subject to sanctions" and lists it as sanctioned in 10 sources, including the US OFAC SDN list, the EU Financial Sanctions Files and the UK FCDO list. It lists Sergey Dokuchaev as chairman of the management board since 1 February 2010.

OpenSanctions records Opaleva as a person in the Russian company register; its page says she "has not been found on international sanctions lists" and is not linked to any risk indications in its database. It shows her holding 33.34% of the Moscow company Legion K LLC since 3 October 2012, with Dokuchaev listed at 33.33% from the same date. The Legion K page says the company has not been found on international sanctions lists; its sanction-ownership tags come from graph-based tagging that the page calls a non-official source.
Opaleva is the museum's founder, and Forbes Russia says she paid for the mansion from her own funds.

name: Fabrika Centre for Creative Industries
overview: Private creative cluster at Perevedenovsky Lane 18, Moscow, in the buildings of the former Oktyabr technical paper factory. It holds artists' studios, exhibition halls, a theatre space and creative businesses.

The cluster opened in 2005 with the "No Comment" project for the First Moscow Biennale. Asya Filippova began work as General Director of the Oktyabr technical paper factory in 2003 and leads the centre (Fabrika's about page).

In the 1870s Elizaveta Andreevna Dislen bought the plot. The partnership was nationalised in 1924, and the plant became a technical paper factory in 1941 (Fabrika's about page). The Oktyabr factory still made technical paper in 2016 (The Art Newspaper Russia).
funding_verdict: Fabrika: self-funded: rent from studios and the Oktyabr paper mill, as stated by director Asya Filippova
wider_context: Novaya Gazeta, Grigory Mirsky, "Жилой или живой? ЦТИ «Фабрика» объявил о скором закрытии" ("Residential or Living? CTI Fabrika Announces Imminent Closure", title translated), 2025: criticises Moscow's comprehensive territorial development programme for treating former industrial zones as "depressive", and argues that redeveloped old factories such as Vinzavod, Flacon, Artplay and GES-2 keep links to the past that demolition does not. It says that in a destroyed civil society institutions like Fabrika cannot count on support against the state machine. The piece does not criticise Fabrika. URL: https://novayagazeta.ru/articles/2025/11/19/zhiloi-ili-zhivoi

Art Focus Now, Ekaterina Wagner, "Farewell to Fabrika: A Transient Oasis of Freedom", 9 February 2026: reports that the city authorities consider the land "ineffective" and plan to demolish the complex for housing, and that appeals to save it were ignored. It quotes curator Mikhail Sidlin calling such spaces "a space of freedom". URL: https://artfocusnow.com/news/farewell-to-fabrika-a-transient-oasis-of-freedom/

name: Museum of Russian Impressionism
overview: Private art museum on the Bolshevik grounds at Leningradsky Prospekt 15, building 11, Moscow (museum website). The permanent exhibition on the second floor shows works by Konstantin Korovin, Valentin Serov, Stanislav Zhukovsky and Nikolai Bogdanov-Belsky (museum website).
Founded by the collector Boris Mints (O1 Group). The museum opened to the public on 28 May 2016, and began in 2014 with exhibitions held by the MacDougall's auction house (Wikipedia).

Building: the museum's own page says it was built in the 1960s to store flour and sugar and converted by the British architects John McAslan + Partners, keeping the cylindrical form and adding a perforated metal cladding, with five floors and about 1,000 square metres of exhibition space. Wikipedia says construction started in 2012 and cost $16.5 million, on the site of a former Bolshevik confectionery factory.
funding_verdict: Museum of Russian Impressionism: private: a patron-trustee, ticket sales and commercial partners

name: Arsenal, Volga-Vyatka branch of the Pushkin Museum
overview: Contemporary art museum inside the Nizhny Novgorod Kremlin, building 6 (Arsenal website).

The institution has run exhibition and interdisciplinary projects since 1997 and has been a branch of the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts since 2020 (Arsenal website). Earlier it was the Nizhny Novgorod branch of the State Centre for Contemporary Art (GTsSI), which was handed the Arsenal building in 2003. The branch has occupied it since 2011 (Kommersant, Citizen K, 2011; Pushkin Museum branch page).

Building: built in 1837 to 1843 to a design by Anton Leer and attached to a 16th-century Kremlin wall. It housed the Defence Ministry's map archive and stood unrepaired for more than 150 years. Evgeny Ass worked on adapting it, and the first phase of about 1,700 square metres had opened by 2011 (Kommersant, Anna Tolstova, 30 May 2011). The Arsenal site calls it an architectural monument of late classicism.
funding_verdict: Arsenal: mainly public: federal funds through the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, with corporate sponsors and family patrons
wider_context: Bank PSB is listed on the Arsenal support page as a partner of the Pushkin Museum. PSB is the abbreviation of Promsvyazbank (Wikipedia), and the Pushkin Museum's board of trustees page lists Promsvyazbank with Pyotr Fradkov as chairman. The board is chaired by Marat Khusnullin, Deputy Chairman of the Government of the Russian Federation, and lists representatives of Sberbank, Gazprombank, Transneft, Sibur and Rosseti (Pushkin Museum board page).
Wikipedia states that the UK announced sanctions against Promsvyazbank on 22 February 2022, that the US also imposed sanctions on it, and that the Russian government nationalised the bank in 2018.

press_items.title: Anna Tolstova, "Отвоеванный Арсенал" ("The Reclaimed Arsenal") (30 May 2011)

name: Tikhaya Studio
overview: Artist-run studio with an exhibition hall and open storage at Ulyanova Street 4 in Nizhny Novgorod (The Blueprint), about three minutes' walk from the Kremlin (RBC Style, 9 August 2024).
Founded in spring 2015 by the artist Artem Filatov, who is its director (RBC Style, 1 May 2025; obdn.ru, 8 September 2022). It opened on the base of art workshops (obdn.ru).

Named for the street's former name, Tikhonovskaya, which came from a church demolished in Soviet times (obdn.ru). RBC Style says Filatov also ties the name to a quiet, hospitable way of dealing with visitors.
funding_verdict: Tikhaya Studio: privately funded: artists' shared rent, patrons' money, and regional and museum grants

name: Manege Central Exhibition Hall
overview: Museum and exhibition complex at Isaakievskaya Square 1, St Petersburg, which calls itself the largest exhibition space in the city centre (Manege website).

The building is a riding hall designed by the Italian architect Giacomo Quarenghi, finished in 1804. The Life Guards Horse Regiment it served was established by decree of Empress Anna Ioannovna in 1730 (Manege website).
After 1917 it became a warehouse and in 1930 to 1932 a garage for state security agencies. It was converted into an exhibition hall in 1973 to 1977 and opened in November 1977 (Manege website).
funding_verdict: Manege: public institution working to a state assignment; its site lists corporate partners and sponsors
